market_context: United States; current trans-fat regulation and labeling
title: Trans Fat: Where It Still Shows Up and How to Spot It

seo.title: Trans Fat: Where It Still Appears Today
seo.meta_description: Partially hydrogenated oils have been removed from the U.S. food supply as an approved ingredient, but small natural trans-fat amounts occur in ruminant meat and dairy.
seo.search_intent: Explain where trans fats can still occur and how current U.S. labels differ from older products.

excerpt: Industrial trans fat has fallen sharply in the U.S. because partially hydrogenated oils are no longer permitted as a standard food ingredient. Small naturally occurring amounts can still be present in meat and dairy from ruminants, and label rounding can make very small per-serving amounts appear as 0 g.
content_html:
Advice from twenty years ago can make trans fat sound like a common hidden ingredient in every cookie and tub of spread. The U.S. food supply has changed substantially. Partially hydrogenated oils, once the major industrial source, are no longer generally recognized as safe for use in food.

Why older products had much more

Partial hydrogenation made liquid oils more solid and shelf-stable, but it also produced trans fatty acids. Those fats raise LDL cholesterol and can lower HDL, which drove regulatory action and reformulation.

Some trans fat occurs naturally

Beef, lamb, butter, and other ruminant foods can contain small amounts formed in the animal's digestive system. That is different from deliberately adding partially hydrogenated oil.

Why a label can say 0 g

Nutrition Facts rules allow very small amounts per serving to be rounded. That means “0 g trans fat” does not necessarily mean chemically zero, although today's industrial exposure is far lower than it once was.

The useful modern habit is to look at saturated fat and the overall food pattern as well, rather than treating every packaged food as a major trans-fat source.

faq.question: Are trans fats banned in the United States?
faq.answer: Partially hydrogenated oils, the former major industrial source, are no longer permitted as a standard approved food ingredient. Tiny natural amounts can still occur.

faq.question: Does butter contain trans fat?
faq.answer: Yes, it can contain small naturally occurring amounts from ruminant fat.

faq.question: Can a food with 0 g trans fat contain a little?
faq.answer: Yes. U.S. labeling rules permit rounding of very small amounts per serving.
